div.p: Fear learning processes are believed to play a crucial role in the development and maintenance of anxiety and stress-related disorders. To integrate results across different studies, we conducted a systematic metaanalysis following PRISMA guidelines to examine differences in fear conditioning during fear acquisition, extinction, and extinction recall between individuals with anxiety-related or stress-related disorders and healthy participants. This analysis updates the work of Duits et al. (2015) while also refining distinctions between physiological and behavioral outcomes and examining extinction recall. Our meta-analysis encompasses 77 studies published from 1986 to 2022, involving 2052 patients with anxiety disorders, OCD, or PTSD, and 3258 healthy controls. The results indicate significant differences in fear acquisition, extinction, and recall between the two groups. Specifically, during acquisition patients exhibited heightened physiological and behavioral responses to the CS-and reported increased affect ratings for the CS+. During extinction and extinction recall, patients continue to show heightened threat expectancy and negative affect ratings towards the CS-and increased affect ratings towards the CS+. No differences were found in CS+/CSdifferentiation between groups. These findings imply that individuals with anxiety and stress-related disorders may exhibit amplified responses to safety cues and stronger reactions to threat cues during fear conditioning, lasting through extinction and extinction recall. These changes may lead to increased sensitivity in detecting fear and slower extinction process, resulting in more enduring anxiety responses. We discuss these results in the context of existing literature on fear and safety learning and consider potential underlying mechanisms.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Acquiring the ability to recognize threats, adapt behavior in response to potential dangers, and protect oneself from harm are fundamental characteristics of human behavior that can be crucial for survival. However, excessive fear and anxiety can lead to behavioral impairments and distress, as seen in individuals affected by anxiety-, stress-related disorders, and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD; American Psychiatric Association, 2013), which are the most prevalent mental health disorders globally (Kessler et al., 2005). Anxiety disorders impose a significant burden on individuals, compromising their overall quality of life, and also carry substantial socioeconomic costs (Konnopka & Konig, 2020;Rehm & Shield, 2019). Alterations in fear and safety learning processes have been identified as crucial in the onset and maintenance of anxiety-and stress-related disorders (Craske et al., 2022;Duits et al., 2015). Exposure-based therapies are an evidence-based and highly effective form of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) 1 for anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and OCD, which specifically target the underlying learning processes (Hofmann & Smits, 2008). However, a significant proportion of individuals do not respond to these treatments, and symptom recurrence is a common phenomenon (Craske & Mystkowski, 2006;Pittig et al., 2021;Springer et al., 2018). Therefore, advancing our understanding of the mechanisms contributing to anxiety and the persistence of anxiety symptoms is crucial for refining existing treatment modalities and developing innovative interventions (Craske et al., 2022).

In laboratory settings, Pavlovian fear conditioning paradigms have emerged as a central tool for investigating fear learning processes, resulting in significant advancements of our basic understanding of the underlying mechanisms, and further enabling researchers to develop and refine effective treatment options (Beckers et al., 2023;Craske et al., 2022;Craske et al., 2014;Vervliet & Boddez, 2020). The core process in fear conditioning involves presenting an initially neutral stimulus (NS), paired with an inherently aversive or threatening stimulus (unconditioned stimulus; US). Through multiple repetitions of this pairing, an association is established between the NS and the US, known as fear acquisition. During fear acquisition, the NS becomes a conditioned fear stimulus (CS+) that can elicit conditioned fear responses in the absence of the US, termed conditioned fear responses (CR; Pavlov, 1927). In the context of differential fear conditioning, a second neutral stimulus is introduced during fear acquisition but is never paired with the US, thereby becoming a safety-associated stimulus (CS-). In addition to the responding to CS+ and CS-, their differentiation, e.g. the difference in response to the CS+ versus the CS-, is a commonly used outcome in fear conditioning studies (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). During extinction learning, the CS+ is presented repeatedly without the aversive US (now CS+/noUS), which leads to a decrease in the CR (Hermans et al., 2006;Milad & Quirk, 2012). More specifically, during fear extinction a new stimulus-outcome association for the CS+, i.e. a safety representation for the absence of the aversive outcome is formed. Studies support the assumption that the original memory trace (CS+/US) is not erased but coexists with the new learning trace (CS+/noUS) but is inhibited by the newly formed association (Kim & Jung, 2006;Myers & Davis, 2007). In addition to the most frequently examined processes of fear acquisition and extinction, some studies also investigate the persistence of extinction learning by incorporating an extinction recall phase. This phase typically occurs either immediately or within a delay, often 24 hours or more, after extinction training and does not involve any active experimental manipulation. During extinction recall, the CS+/noUS is presented again to test whether the extinction memory is retrieved and expressed (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). The purpose of this phase is to evaluate whether extinction retention occurs, indicating either the maintenance of extinction or a spontaneous renewal or recovery of the conditioned fear response (CR). Essentially, it assesses whether the fear memory or the extinction memory trace is dominant. This phase is particularly interesting from a clinical perspective, considering the frequent reports of the recurrence of anxiety, OCD, or PTSD symptoms after successful exposure therapy (Levy et al., 2021).

The formation of associations and the learning process, i.e., whether fear and safety learning have occurred, can be investigated at various levels, including verbal reports on affective experiences, cognitive evaluation, physiological responses, and neurobiological mechanisms (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). According to the dual-process account of fear learning (Hamm & Weike, 2005;LeDoux & Pine, 2016;Sevenster et al., 2012), distinct learning processes are at work that can be assessed through different outcome measures. More specifically, this framework posits the existence of two emotional learning systems in fear responses: a rapid, automatic system responsible for reflexive fear reactions, such as physiological responses, and a slower, controlled system involved in cognitive fear responses that consider contextual information and previous experiences, as measured through ratings. This highlights the significance of incorporating diverse measurements and units of analysis for a comprehensive understanding of fear and safety learning.

Verbal reports of the affective valence of the CS+ and CS-as well as cognitive evaluations of threat expectancy occurrence are among the most common outcome measures in the fear conditioning domain (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). On a psychophysiological level, skin conductance responses (SCRs) and fear potentiated startle (FPS) represent commonly utilized indices of fear conditioning (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). Both represent bodily responses mediated by the autonomic nervous system (Davis, 2006;Dawson et al., 2007). SCR captures the electrical conductivity of the skin that is influenced by sweat production and is a marker of sympathetic arousal (Bradley et al., 2001).

Typically, fear acquisition leads to increased SCRs for the CS+ (Lonsdorf et al., 2017), that decrease during fear extinction (Sperl et al., 2021). FPS is defined as heightened electromyographic activity of the orbicularis oculi during the startle reflex in response to acoustic stimuli (e.g., white noise burst) when fear is present (i.e., CS+) (Blumenthal et al., 2005). On a neural level, FPS is initiated primarily in brainstem structures (Davis, 2007;Gomez-Nieto et al., 2014;Lee et al., 1996;Lipp, 2006), and modulated by the amygdala and dorsomedial PFC/ACC (Hamm & Weike, 2005).
FPS has been related to the aversiveness or negative valence of a stimuli (Bradley et al., 1999).

Additional physiological and neuroanatomical outcome measures commonly used include pupil dilation, heart rate, as well as EEG and fMRI measurements (Lonsdorf et al., 2017). Brain imaging has increasingly clarified the mechanisms underlying fear acquisition and extinction. Fear acquisition primarily relies on the "fear network," notably involving the basolateral and centromedial nuclei of the amygdala, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and the insula (Büchel & Dolan, 2000;Craske et al., 2022;Fullana et al., 2016;Namkung et al., 2022). The brain networks involved in fear extinction learning overlap with these regions and also include the hippocampus and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Bouton et al., 2021;Büchel & Dolan, 2000;Fullana et al., 2018;Fullana et al., 2016;Hermann et al., 2016;Kim & Jung, 2006;Milad & Quirk, 2012). In summary, fear conditioning studies offer a valuable experimental framework that deepens our understanding of fear learning and extinction, holding high clinical relevance and translational potential across species and from laboratory research to clinical applications. The different outcome measures, such as physiological responses, imaging data, and self-report questionnaires, highlight various processes and aspects of fear conditioning. Together, they allow for a comprehensive evaluation of fear-related phenomena, facilitating a more nuanced understanding of both the mechanistic underpinnings and the therapeutic implications of anxiety-and stress-related disorders.

Scientific literature and models of PTSD, OCD and anxiety psychopathology highlight that individuals with anxiety-or stress-related disorders exhibit alterations across multiple facets and phases of fear conditioning, including fear acquisition, generalization, extinction, and extinction recall (Cooper et al., 2022;Craske et al., 2014;Duits et al., 2015;Fraunfelter et al., 2022;Lissek et al., 2005;Milad & Quirk, 2012). Findings published up to 2013 have been summarized and integrated in the influential meta-analysis by Duits et al. (2015) that offers a valuable synthesis of findings and insight in psychopathological mechanisms underlying anxiety. First, it suggests that patients with an anxiety-or stress-related disorder show an exaggerated fear response to safety cues (CS-) rather than an increased response to actual threatening cues (CS+). Second, patients with anxiety-or stress-related disorders exhibit increased fear responses to the conditioned fear stimuli (CS+) during extinction, suggesting impairments in fear extinction learning (Duits et al., 2015).

Patients with PTSD were overrepresented in this analysis; however, follow-up analyses suggest that the reported pattern of results holds for both PTSD patients and those with other anxiety-related disorders, including OCD.

The meta-analyses by Duits et al. (2015) has stimulated further research efforts since its release, culminating in many new studies and insights. These studies often support specific changes in fear and safety learning among patients with PTSD, OCD, or other anxiety-related disorders.

However, there is significant heterogeneity in the findings both within specific diagnostic categories and across various anxiety-and stress-related disorders. For instance, whereas studies involving patients with PTSD consistently revealed altered fear acquisition compared with healthy participants as indexed with subjective ratings (Diener et al., 2016;Jenewein et al., 2016;Jovanovic et al., 2009) and FPS (Jovanovic et al., 2010;Jovanovic et al., 2009), results are more mixed for other disorders. In the context of OCD, there is mixed evidence regarding alterations in fear acquisition, but stronger evidence exists for impaired extinction learning (Cooper & Dunsmoor, 2021).. Instead, for patients with social anxiety disorder (SAD) a general increased fear/arousal to both the CS+ and CS-has been reported rather than specific increased responding to the CS- (Ahrens et al., 2016). In addition to heterogeneity in results pattern, significant heterogeneity exists in methodology and in the ways, fear learning and extinction have been measured across these studies. Furthermore, studies directly comparing different clinical groups are limited, but they suggest that differential patterns in fear and safety learning may help distinguish between disorders.

For instance, one study found that PTSD patients exhibited impaired safety learning and extinction, whereas patients with other anxiety disorders did not show these impairments, as measured through subjective ratings and the FPS response (Acheson et al., 2015). Together, these studies demonstrate substantial heterogeneity in findings across conventional ICD/DSM anxiety-or stress-related disorder categories and underscores the importance of conducting more detailed analyses of fear and safety learning within the spectrum of anxiety and stress-related disorders. It underscores the necessity for an updated meta-analysis to integrate more recent findings and to provide a synthesis of current research in this field. Furthermore, the integration of additional studies enables us to extend the previous analyses. More specifically, this involves integrating results for different outcomes separately (i.e., expectancy ratings, affect ratings, FPS, and SCR) as opposed to the broader differentiation between physiological and subjective measures in Duits et al. (2015) analyses. Further, we will examine the differences between anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD.
Additionally, results from extinction recall studies will be integrated and summarized for the first time.

Of note, contemporary models of psychopathology (e.g. HiTOP / RDoC) have gained importance since the initial meta-analysis of Duits et al. (2015). These models highlight the value of looking beyond primary diagnoses, as comorbidity is frequent and within-diagnosis heterogeneity is substantial (Cuthbert & Kozak, 2013;Insel et al., 2010;Kotov et al., 2017). Depressive disorders are the most common comorbid disorders for conditions associated with anxiety-and stress-related disorders (Saha et al., 2020). Consequently, alterations in fear and safety learning that are related to depressive symptoms may also influence the observed patterns of results. Previous research indicated attenuated fear acquisition, as measured with SCR, in individuals with depression (Luo et al., 2024;Otto et al., 2014). Additionally, an increased reactivity to the CS + during extinction learning has been reported in depressed and anhedonic individuals (Wurst et al., 2021;Young et al., 2021). In light of this context, we will include dimensional measures of anxiety and depressive symptom severity, to elucidate the influence of these transdiagnostic dimensions to altered fear and safety learning in the current meta-analysis. Alongside, we will also consider other factors identified in the literature as moderators. We will analyze the influence of US type, CS type, and reinforcement rate as moderators. Previous studies have shown that the US type (e.g., shock, sound) lead to differences in responding. For example, it has been reported that during fear acquisition a scream compared to a shock as the US led to higher reported induced anxiety, lower SCR as well as a more rapid habituation (Ney et al., 2023). Findings reported for different types of CS are rather mixed (e.g., Ahs et al., 2018) with different studies comparing fear relevant (e.g., pictures of spiders or snakes, angry or fearful faces) with neutral stimuli (e.g., geometrical stimuli, neutral faces). A recent systematic review and meta-analysis reported higher SCRs for fear-relevant faces compared to neutral faces (Ney et al., 2022). Lastly, the CS can be paired with the US in 100% of the trials (100% reinforcement rate) or only partially (partial reinforcement). It has been reported that partial reinforcement compared to 100% reinforcement leads to prolonged extinction learning but also reduced response frequency as well as CR amplitudes (for an overview see Lonsdorf et al., 2017).

In the lights of these findings, we will include US type, CS type and reinforcement rate as moderators in our analyses. In the present paper we integrate findings of fear and safety learning in stress-related, anxiety-related psychopathology and OCD using a series of meta-analyses to examine differences in fear acquisition, extinction, and extinction recall for the CS+, CS-, and their discrimination (CS+ minus CS-). Separate meta-analyses will be performed for SCR, FPS, affect and expectancy ratings. Further, the moderating influence of diagnostic category, depressive symptoms, anxiety symptom severity, US type, CS type, and reinforcement rate were considered based on their empirically supported influences.

div.head: Study selection
div.p: The review was conducted in adherence to the PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021). Building on the study selection procedure by Duits et al. (2015), we conducted a systematic database search for journal articles published until December 2022 on PubMed. We based our search terms on that of Duits et al. (2015), but modified the search string to include further keywords related to anxietyand stress-related disorders, ensuring better representation of all anxiety-and stress-related disorders. The final search string was: "(conditioned OR conditioning) AND (conditioning OR conditioned OR anxiety OR anxious OR fear) AND (PTSD OR post-traumatic stress disorder OR posttraumatic OR phobic OR phobia OR panic OR OCD) AND (patient AND/OR disorder)". These terms were required to appear in the title and/or abstract of the papers. No language restrictions were imposed. Figure 1 shows the study flow chart of our selection process. During this process, three independent master students conducted the database search. If inconsistencies between the students occurred, they were checked and resolved by the first author. The search strategy yielded 1660 studies, which were imported into EndNoteData. Each abstract was assessed based on the following inclusion criteria:
1. Inclusion of adult patients (age ≥ 18 years) with anxiety disorders, OCD, and PTSD, as defined according to DSM criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), as well as healthy participants.
2. Diagnosis of a disorder was established through formal diagnostic interviewing. A selfscreening tool was not sufficient.
3. Examination of classical aversive conditioning, at least a phase of fear acquisition had to be present.

4. In addition to fear acquisition, we included studies that investigated fear extinction, and extinction recall, without an experimental manipulation (e.g., reinstatement). 5. Use of subjective (e.g., ratings of US-expectancy or fear) and/or psychophysiological (FPS, SCR, pupil dilation, heart rate) outcome measurements to assess conditioned fear responses.

Following abstract screening, 1489 articles had to be excluded for several reasons such as metaanalysis or review, genetic study, study in animals, pharmacological manipulation, or no fear conditioning study, leaving 171 studies for full text screening. Of those, 85 studies qualify to be included in the meta-analyses. Because 21 studies did not provide sufficient statistical details to calculate the effect sizes, we reached out to corresponding authors. Although we sent several requests, only five labs provided the requested data. In addition, we were able to extract data from figures in eight studies using WebPlotDigitizer (Rohatgi, 2022). Ultimately, we had to exclude eight studies from the current meta-analysis because the reported statistics did not offer the necessary information to compute or estimate the effect sizes leaving us with 77 included studies in the meta-analyses. div.head: Meta-analysis
div.p: The data were analyzed using R version 4.3.2 (R Core Team, 2023) and RStudio version 2023.06.1 (RStudio Team, 2023). A p-value of .05 was defined as the significance threshold.

To calculate the meta-analytic models, the packages dmetar (version 0.1.0; (Harrer et al., 2021), and meta (version 6.5-0; (Balduzzi et al., 2019) were used. The code and data used for the analyses are accessible at www.osf/TBA .

As an index of effect sizes, we used the standardized between-group mean difference (SMD). Here, SMD represents the mean difference in fear responses between anxiety patients and healthy participants, standardized by the pooled standard deviation. Thereby, data across studies could be combined and analyzed, independent of their operationalization. We estimated the SMD using Hedges' g formula to correct for small sample bias (Hedges, 1981).

The way we analyzed our data, positive values indicate stronger responses in anxiety patients, whereas negative values indicate stronger responses in healthy participants. Effect sizes were pooled separately per experimental phase (i.e., acquisition, extinction, and extinction recall), per outcome (i.e., SCR, startle reflex, expectancy ratings, and affect ratings), and per cue (i.e., responses to CS+, responses to CS-, ΔCS). To assess ΔCS (i.e., the difference between CS+ minus CS-) we calculated standardized difference scores per original study, group (i.e., clinical sample and healthy control group), phase, and outcome by calculating hedges g between CS+ and CS-and using the M of the

SDs of CS+/CS-. Random effect models were used due to the anticipated substantial between-study heterogeneity and assumed variance in true effects. We expected that potential variation would mainly be introduced in true effects by heterogeneity in the clinical samples and methodological heterogeneity in the experimental protocols. To calculate the heterogeneity variance τ 2 , the restricted maximum likelihood estimator was used (Viechtbauer, 2005). The weight given to each study was the inverse of the variance of the effect estimate. To calculate the confidence interval around the pooled effect (using the Q-profile method; (Viechtbauer, 2007), Knapp-Hartung adjustments were used (Knapp & Hartung, 2003). To investigate variation in the included studies, we estimated between-study heterogeneity (i.e., statistical heterogeneity) of the pooled effect sizes and reported Higgins & Thompson's I 2 statistic, which can be interpreted with I 2 = 25%: low heterogeneity, I 2 = 50%: moderate heterogeneity, and I 2 = 75%: substantial heterogeneity (Higgins & Thompson, 2002).

div.head: Moderator analyses
div.p: To identify possible sources of statistical heterogeneity, we performed follow-up subgroup analyses and meta-regressions if k ≥ 10 studies reported any of our pre-defined moderator variables for CS+, CS-and ΔCS (Harrer et al., 2021). Subgroup-specific effects were analyzed for categories that had at least 5 studies for each CS+, CS-and ΔCS. The numbers of moderators considered in the analyses differed between phases, outcomes and stimuli. In general, the most moderators could be analyzed for subjective ratings and acquisition, while the number of studies for physiological outcomes was often insufficient to perform subgroup analyses. Table S3 in the supplement displays the number of studies we could include for the subgroup analyses, and hence which subgroup analyses were conducted. Subgroup analyses included omnibus Q-tests indicating whether subgroup differences are large enough not to be explainable by sampling error (Harrer et al., 2021) which were followed-up by calculating effect sizes per level of subgroup separately. Moderators include experimental factors (i.e., US-type, reinforcement rate, and CS-type) and sample characteristics (i.e., diagnostic group, depressive symptoms and anxiety symptoms; see table 1 and 2 for detailed information regarding the moderators). Specifically, to assess potential moderating effects of depressive or anxiety symptoms, the SMD between patient group and healthy control group were calculated within each primary study, if data of trait anxiety, state anxiety (STAI-T and STAI-S scores; Spielberger et al., 1983), or depression questionnaire, i.e. BDI (Beck et al., 1996), HAM-D (Hamilton, 1960), CES-D (Radloff, 1977), ADS (Meyer & Hautzinger, 2001), IDS-SR (Rush et al., 1986), DASS-D (Nilges & Essau, 2021) were reported. This SMD of depressive, state or trait anxiety symptoms within the primary study represents the extent to which the patient group and healthy control group differ in the respective symptom dimension and was used to examine potential influences on task effects (i.e., fear conditioning processes). This enables testing potential moderating effects of dimensional clinical measures across different questionnaires used to assess the same construct using meta-regression. Our main interest was to compare anxiety-and stressrelated disorder categories. Due to the overrepresentation of PTSD studies in contrast to all other anxiety-related disorders and OCD, we performed subgroup analyses and compared healthy participants vs. PTSD studies as well as healthy participants vs. all other anxiety-related disorders including OCD, following the approach of Duits et al. If number of studies within each single diagnostic category was at least 5, we also performed diagnose specific subgroup analyses. If more than one experimental condition was reported in a primary study, i.e., if different anxiety groups were included (e.g. see Grillon et al., 2009;Klahn et al., 2017) the comparisons were included twice but the healthy participant sample was divided by 2 to correct for multiple testing within one group following the methodological approach of the meta-analysis by Duits et al. (Duits et al., 2015).

div.head: Outlier analysis and small sample bias assessment
div.p: To assess the robustness of our results, we performed a basic outlier analysis using the function find.outliers which is included in the dmetar package (Harrer et al., 2021). Here, an outlier is detected when its confidence interval does not overlap with the confidence interval of the pooled effect. In our results section, we report the results after outlier analysis and after exclusion of outlying studies. Since the number of outliers was relatively high and to allow the reader to assess the model without outlier removal, we presented the results of the main analyses without outlier removal in the supplement S2, highlighting discrepancies with another font color and refer in the text to discrepancies between these two types of analysis. Additionally, especially in the area of moderator analyses, many models could not be computed due to the insufficient number of studies available after outlier exclusion during certain phases or for specific stimuli. On one hand, the relatively conservative standards we set for the inclusion of studies ensure the robustness of the results and reduce the overall already high number of findings to those with higher robustness. On the other hand, by excluding outliers in the moderator analyses, we also reduce variance that could potentially be explained by our moderators. Thus, all moderator analyses for the full model with all datasets are included in the supplement, and we provide a brief description of the model in the paper. In addition, we examined the presence of publication bias focusing on small-study effects by assessing asymmetry in funnel plots and applying Egger's regression test (Egger et al., 1997) of the intercept, to quantify the presence of funnel plot asymmetry. The intercept of the linear model represents the relationship of the standardized effect sizes to precision; in the absence of publication bias, the intercept is expected to be zero (Harrer et al., 2021). The presence of potential bias was indicated in the respective result sections. Moreover, we conducted p-curve analyses, since it is assumed that they represent more accurately the true effect size behind the data (Simonsohn et al., 2014). We used the function that is included in the dmetar package (Harrer et al., 2021). Due to its sensitivity to between-study heterogeneity, it's proposed to only use p-curve when heterogeneity is small to moderate (as a rule of thumb, i.e. I² < 50%) (van Aert et al., 2016).

div.head: Results
div.p: In total, we included 77 studies, published between 1986 and 2022, resulting in data of 2052 patients with anxiety disorders and 3258 healthy participants (mean age = 34.45, 49.71 % female).

The majority of studies (n = 40) included patients with PTSD, and n = 12 studies compared patients with PD with healthy participants (HC). For all other anxiety disorders less than ten studies were included in the meta-analysis (n = 9 GAD, n = 7 OCD, n = 7 SAD, n = 6 SP). In addition, n = 7 studies included multiple anxiety disorders without specifying the exact sample size per diagnostic category (Mixed anxiety group, MIX). Note that nine studies included more than one diagnostic group, why the number of diagnostic groups is higher than the number of included studies (i.e. Acheson et al., 2015;Fyer et al., 2020;Grillon et al., 2009;Klahn et al., 2017;Marin et al., 2020;Otto et al., 2014;Pohlchen et al., 2020;Rabinak et al., 2017;Tinoco-Gonzalez et al., 2015). For an overview of the included studies and their key experimental characteristics, see table 3. For a more detailed overview of the included studies (i.e., details regarding age, gender distribution, anxiety, and depressive symptoms), see table S1 in the supplement.

Not all studies included in our analysis examined all experimental phases or used the same behavioral and physiological measures, leading to variations in the number of observations in each analysis (986 to 2500 data points, i.e., sample size in primary study). We analyzed data from 18 to 54 studies for the acquisition phase (see table 4), 5 to 27 studies for the extinction phase (see table 5), and 2 to 15 studies for the extinction recall phase (see table 6). Outcome measurements are grey colored when they were reported in the primary study but not investigated by the present meta-analysis.

div.head: Acquisition phase
div.p: Table 4 displays the integrated effect size, 95% confidence interval, the estimation of betweenstudy heterogeneity I² and statistical values for the observed group differences for CS+, CS-, as well as ΔCS separately for the different outcome measurements during the acquisition phase, after outlier analyses. Forest plots visualizing the effect sizes of the contributing primary studies and the heterogeneity are presented separately by outcome for CS+ and CS-, as well as for ΔCS in supplementary material accompanying this article in figure S1.

Results suggest no difference in response to the CS+, on physiological level (SCR and FPS), or regarding US expectancy (all p ≥ .20). However, anxiety patients seem to show increased negative affect towards the CS+ compared with healthy participants as suggested by affect ratings (g = 0.52; 95% CI: 0.30-0.74; p < .001). Regarding the CS-, results showed significant higher responses in anxiety patients compared to healthy participants across multiple outcome measurements, i.e., FPS (g = 0.29; 95% CI: 0.16-0.42; p < .001), US expectancy (g = 0.29; 95% CI: 0.14-0.43; p < .001), and affect ratings (g = 0.36; 95% CI: 0.20-0.52; p < .001). Patients and healthy participants did not differ regarding their SCR in response to the CS-. Regarding ΔCS, results suggest no differences between patients and healthy participants in any of our outcome measurements (all p ≥ .066).

In sum, it seems that anxiety patients compared to healthy participants do not respond significantly differently to a threat associated stimulus on a psychophysiological and cognitive level, but they subjectively indicate to experience increased negative affect to a threatening stimulus, i.e. CS+. In contrast, multiple outcome measures suggest that anxiety patients seem to associate an actual safe stimulus (CS-) with increased fear on cognitive, subjective and partly psychophysiological levels (FPS). This implies that anxiety patients may have impairments in regulating their fear in response to a safe stimulus. The results for ΔCS did not indicate any consistent differences in fear acquisition across any of the outcome measures. Heterogeneity was low to moderate for the CS-analyses (I² = 0-46%), moderate to high for the CS+ (I² = 28-61 %), and with one exception mostly high for the ΔCS (I² = 0-93 %), underscoring the need for additional moderator analyses.

The results of the full model, which includes all studies without excluding outliers (see table S2 in the supplement), are consistent, except for an additional effect observed for ΔCS measured with FPS, indicating a reduced differentiation between CS+ and CS-in patients with stress-related and anxiety-related disorders compared to healthy participants. However, as expected, there was substantial heterogeneity across all stimuli in all outcome measurements (I² = 8-93%). for the subgroup analyses were significant. Regarding the CS+, there was a significant difference between groups for affect ratings (p = .006). We obtained a significant subgroup-specific effect for the anxiety disorders and OCD group (g = 0.73, p < .001), suggesting significant higher affect ratings for the CS+ for anxiety and OCD patients compared with healthy participants and the PTSD group which did not differ from healthy participants. This suggests that individuals with an anxiety disorder or OCD may give increased affect ratings to the CS+, an effect that is not observed in PTSD. Regarding the CS-, results showed a significant difference between subgroups in US expectancy ratings (p = .002). Follow-up analyses revealed subgroup-specific effects for both groups (PTSD: g = 0.12, p = .021; Anxiety disorders and OCD: g = 0.58, p = .003), suggesting significantly higher US expectancy rating towards the CS-in both groups. Notably, patients with anxiety disorders and OCD demonstrated significantly stronger effects, reflecting larger effect sizes and higher US expectancy ratings to the CS-compared to those with PTSD. Regarding the ΔCS, we found a significant difference between groups in SCR responses (p = .035). For PTSD, the subgroup-specific effect was not significant, indicating no difference in ΔCS responding compared to healthy individuals. There was a significant effect for the group anxiety disorders and OCD (g = 0.92, p = .036), suggesting a significant greater difference of SCR responding in ΔCS for anxiety and OCD patients compared to healthy participants.

In summary, our findings indicate that for most measures the pattern of results observed during the acquisition phase is not significantly different for patients with OCD and anxiety compared to those with PTSD. However, some exceptions have to be noted where the two groups differed. Follow-up analyses support significant differences between anxiety and OCD for ΔCS for the SCR responding, for CS-for expectancy ratings, and for CS+ and CS-for affect ratings.
Notably, in all these cases, effect sizes and differences were larger for the anxiety/OCD group compared to healthy controls, while they were smaller or even non-significant for the PTSD group.

Overall, there was a highly varying between-study heterogeneity in both groups across almost all outcome measures (I² = 0. 95%) indicating large variability among studies, underscoring the importance of investigating potential moderators.

Results of the full model (see table S2 in the supplement) revealed a similar pattern, but fewer subgroup analyses reached significance, with many p-values narrowly missing the significance threshold. Additionally, a subgroup effect was observed for CS+ and CS-measured with SCR (both p ≤ 0.050), although both subgroups did not significantly differ from the healthy participants in follow-up analyses. Again, substantial heterogeneity was noted across all analyses (I² = 81-87%). These differences in subgroup effects between the full model and the one without outliers indicate that they are more influenced by the exclusion of studies compared to the main findings, warranting greater caution regarding the robustness of these results.

div.head: Moderator Analyses: Experimental factors and sample characteristics
div.p: Following our criterion of having at least k ≥ 10 studies for dimensional, and k ≥ 5 studies for categorical moderator-analyses, we were able to analyze the following moderators in the acquisition phase: reinforcement rate for all outcomes, trait anxiety for all but FPS and depression for both ratings (US expectancy and affective ratings, see supplementary table S3).

Detailed statistics are available in table S4 in the supplement. Two moderators significantly influenced the results for ΔCS in SCR and FPS. Results indicate that trait anxiety affected responses for ΔCS in SCR (F(1,9) = 8.41, p = .018), specifically showing increasing effect sizes with increasing trait anxiety. The higher the difference of anxiety symptoms between patients and healthy participants, the smaller the difference between CS+ and CS-(figure 2). Furthermore, reinforcement rate influenced responses for ΔCS in FPS (F(1,17) = 7.23, p = .016), suggesting larger effect sizes for FPS responses with increasing reinforcement rates. All other moderators examined in the present analysis did not reach significance (all p > .082). Overall, the results suggest that variability in outcomes cannot be attributed to the moderating influences of the analyzed variables. Thus, the effect sizes remain consistent across different study characteristics.

As previously described, the outlier analysis led to many subgroup analyses being unfeasible. Therefore, we report in the supplement in Table S5 the full model without excluding outliers. Even here, the number of studies in some cells was too low, but we were able to conduct significantly more analyses. The relationship reported in the corrected model between reinforcement rate and the FPS effect in the ΔCS was replicated; however, the STAI effect for ΔCS SCR response was not replicated (p = .338). Additionally, other moderating influences emerged during the acquisition phase. The CS type moderated the effects in the expectancy rating for the CS+, with higher effect sizes observed for pictures and shapes than for the CS-. An influence of the US type on the affect rating of the CS-was also noted; the effect was smaller for visual stimuli and sounds compared to electrotactile stimulation and combinations. This was also reflected in an influence on the ΔCS, which showed less differentiation for these US types. There were no significant findings related to diagnosis-specific influences, which could only be investigated in relation to affect ratings. For the dimensional analyses, additional effects were found concerning the relationship between depressive symptoms and the response to the CS+ in the SCR, as well as the reinforcement rate related to the CS+ SCR response. Increased SCR responses to the CS+ were associated with larger differences in depressive symptoms between the anxiety disorder/OCD group and healthy participant group. A larger SCR response to the CS+ was observed with a higher reinforcement rate, similar to the effect seen with the FPS on ΔCS.

div.head: Extinction phase
div.p: In table 5, results of the main model, i.e. the comparison of fear extinction between healthy participants and patients with anxiety-and stress-related disorders for CS+, CS-and ΔCS are shown. Forest plots visualizing the effect sizes of the contributing primary studies and the heterogeneity are presented separately by outcome in supplementary material accompanying this article in figure S2. Compared to healthy participants, patients with anxiety, stress-related disorders and OCD showed increased fear during extinction in affect ratings to both stimuli, i.e., the former threatening stimulus, as well as the safe stimulus (CS+: g = 0.93, p = .024; CS-: g = 0.37, p < .001).

Regarding the ratings of US expectancy, anxiety patients showed increased fear to the safe stimulus, i.e. CS-: g = 0.19, p = .001. Focusing on psychophysiological outcomes, i.e. SCR and FPS, we did not find any significant differences between groups. In addition, regarding the ΔCS, there was no significant difference between groups in any of our outcome measurements. In sum, results suggest that patients with stress-related and anxiety-related disorders compared with healthy participants seem to have difficulties in fear extinction learning on a behavioral level as reflected in higher affect ratings to the CS+. Furthermore, they report exaggerated threat (US) expectancy and affect responses to the CS-. The increased responsiveness to the CS+ in affective ratings that was observed during the acquisition phase persists during the extinction phase, just as the safety stimulus CS-also continued to be rated as more aversive in the affect and expectancy rating by patients with anxiety-and stress-related disorders. This might indicate that patients with stressrelated and anxiety-related disorders have difficulties to limit their acquired fear to the CS+, which seems to hold at least for the time of extinction training. For the reported models after outlier exclusion, heterogeneity was quite mixed (I² = 0-98%).

Results of the full model before outlier exclusion (see table S6 in the supplement) are very similar, as they also show increased responding of patients to the CS-in affect and US expectancy ratings (both p ≤ 0.041). In addition, in the full model SCRs also indicate increased responding after extinction training to the CS-for patients with anxiety, PTSD and OCD (p = .041). In contrast to the model after outlier exclusion, there is no increased responding in affect ratings to the CS+ of anxiety patients. Importantly, there was again substantial heterogeneity in almost all analyses (I² = 52-99%), apart from a few exceptions. Overall, the reported pattern of results is consistent between the model with and without outlier exclusion, which supports the robustness of the analyses.

div.head: Moderator Analyses: Subgroup analyses PTSD vs. other anxiety disorders
div.p: During the extinction phase, subgroup analyses suggest a significant difference in FPS responses to the CS+ and ΔCS between PTSD patients and those with anxiety disorders and OCD (both p ≤ 0.009). For both stimuli CS+ and ΔCS, we obtained a significant subgroup-specific effect for the PTSD group (CS+: g = 0.56, p = .038, n = 3; ΔCS: g = 1.21, p < .001, n = 1), which was absent for anxiety and OCD. So while no overall effects were observed for FPS, PTSD patients showed elevated FPS to the CS+ and ΔCS. Please note the limited number of studies included. Also, note that other subgroup effects did not reach statistical significance. For completeness, the table includes follow-up analyses for both groups separately in these instances as well; however, we refrain from interpreting these results. The estimated between-study heterogeneity varied strongly in both groups (I² = 0-98%), suggesting large variety between studies (table 5 depicts detailed statistics).
Analyses including outliers (see table S6 in the supplement) show a similar pattern of results, suggesting that PTSD patients show larger ΔCS responses in FPS, however not to the CS+.
In addition, we observed a stronger responding to the CS-in SCR in PTSD.

div.head: Moderator Analyses: Experimental factors and sample characteristics
div.p: The following moderators were analyzed during extinction in the model after outlier exclusion:

reinforcement rate for US expectancy and affective ratings (see supplementary table S7) and depression score for affective ratings. In sum, we did not find any significant effect of any of the moderators. In contrast to the reduced model, the full model without outlier exclusion revealed several significant moderating influences, as detailed in Table S9 of the supplement. Similar to the acquisition phase, both CS and US type moderated the findings, with stronger effects observed for pictures as the CS type in the SCR response to CS+. The US type also moderated the CS+ response, with stronger effects noted for electrotactile stimulations in the affect rating. No effects were found for diagnosis-specific influences, which could only be analyzed in relation to affect ratings.

Regarding dimensional predictors, an influence of reinforcement rate on the CS-SCR response was observed, with higher responses during extinction being associated with a higher reinforcement rate during acquisition. Additionally, depressive symptoms influenced affect ratings for CS-and the ΔCS. Increased affect ratings for CS-were associated with larger differences in depression scores between the anxiety/OCD groups and healthy participant groups. In contrast, larger differences in depression scores between the anxiety/OCD groups and healthy participant groups were associated with smaller ΔCS affect ratings (Table S9), possibly explained by a descriptive influence of increased depression score differences on smaller CS+ affect ratings, which was beyond the significance threshold.

div.head: Extinction recall phase
div.p: In contrast to fear acquisition and fear extinction, fear extinction recall has only been investigated in a limited number of studies (see table 6). In line with the other phases, we also performed outlier analyses and report results after those analyses. However, outliers were only detected for SCRs.

Therefore, we created only one table, including the results with and without outliers. Forest plots visualizing the effect sizes of the contributing primary studies and the heterogeneity are presented separately by outcome for CS+ and CS-, and ΔCS in supplementary material accompanying this article in figure S5. Patients with anxiety-and stress-related disorders seem to have ongoing aberrancies in fear extinction learning in subjective ratings as indicated by increased ratings to the CS-(US expectancy: g = 0.37, 95% CI: 0.05-0.69; p = .030, affect rating: g = 0.30, 95% CI: 0.11-0.50; p = .007) compared with healthy participants during extinction recall. In addition, again increased affect ratings for the CS+ were observed in patients (g = 0.46, 95% CI: -0.21-0.72; p = .003). Regarding the SCR, results indicate increased responding to the CS+ in patients with anxietyand stress-related disorders in extinction recall (g = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.01-0.55; p = .044). In contrast, patients with anxiety disorders, PTSD and OCD do not seem to show exaggerated fear, as measured via FPS. Results even suggest increased responding for healthy participants to the CS-during extinction recall (g = -0.21, 95% CI: -0.23-(-0.20); p = .004). However, since only two studies contributed to this finding, the interpretative power is limited, and we will not discuss the effect in depth. Overall, analyses of the extinction recall phase mirror results of the extinction phase, indicating persistent difficulties in learning the new safety association, effect sizes are overall small, and only the increased responding to the CS+ in affective ratings was of medium effect size (Hedges, 1981). Between-study heterogeneity was rather low (I² = 0-47%), indicating the reliability of these results (Ryan, 2016). Due to the limited number of studies, we were not able to conduct subgroup analyses for the extinction recall phase. A graphical representation of the effect sizes, as well as a summary of the results across all phases (i.e, acquisition, extinction, and extinction recall), separately for different outcome measures and CS+. CS-and ΔCS can be found in figures 3 and 4, respectively.
