div.head: Publication bias
div.p: To investigate publication bias, we visually inspected the funnel plots of the effect sizes of all outcome measurements for both stimuli (see figure S3 and S4 in the supplement). In addition, we performed an Egger's test to test for asymmetry in the funnel plot. For the acquisition phase, the Egger's intercept of the funnel plot was significant for ΔCS measured with SCR (B = 4.91, p = .044), and US expectancy rating (B = -4.52, p = .005), indicating evidence of publication bias. For the extinction phase, publication bias is indicated for the distribution of US expectancy effect sizes for the CS+ (B = 9.66, p = .004), and the CS-(B = 0.82, p = .004). In these cases, it must be considered that the effect sizes reported here are likely overestimated due to publication bias. In addition, we performed p-curve analyses. Because of the heterogeneity in our data, it was only possible to conduct those analyses for some but not all outcome measures. Therefore, we refer interested readers to the results of the analyses in the supplement (figure S3 and S4).

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Considering the significance attributed to fear and safety learning in both pathophysiological models and therapeutic strategies for anxiety and related disorders (Kitt et al., 2023;Mineka & Oehlberg, 2008;Pittig et al., 2018), our objective was to integrate the outcomes of fear conditioning studies investigating fear and safety learning in individuals with anxiety disorders, OCD and PTSD.

Building upon the meta-analysis by Duits et al. (2015), we integrated findings across anxiety-and stress-related disorders, and we conducted additional analyses separately for PTSD vs. anxiety disorders and OCD. Furthermore, we integrated results of different outcome measurements separately for affect ratings, expectancy ratings, FPS and SCR. In total, 77 fear conditioning studies are included in the present meta-analysis, comprising n = 5310 individuals (2052 patients with anxiety disorders, OCD, or PTSD, and 3258 healthy participants). Key findings are:

(1) During fear acquisition, when participants initially learn about the association between a cue and a threat, no significant differences in the physiological responses or expectancy ratings to the CS+ between patients with stress -and anxiety-related disorders and healthy participants emerge. However, patients with stress-and anxiety-related disorders tend to affectively rate the threatening stimulus CS+ as more aversive, an effect driven by patients with anxiety and OCD specifically. Simultaneously, in the context of fear acquisition, the CS-(a cue that was never paired with a US) leads to an elevated FPS, increased threat expectancy, and greater affect ratings in individuals with stress-and anxiety-related disorders compared to healthy participants. Note that the effects sizes for the observed group differences during acquisition are small (US-expectancy rating, FPS) to moderate (affect ratings). When comparing patients with PTSD vs. anxiety and OCD most effects hold for both clinical groups, even though the effects were larger for anxiety/OCD. Further, only anxiety patients and OCD but not PTSD patients show an elevated SCR response to the ΔCS as well as elevated affect ratings to the CS+ (large effect sizes).

(2) During fear extinction, after the formerly threatening stimulus (CS+) is no longer paired with a threat, individuals with anxiety-and stress-related disorders continue to show heightened threat expectancy towards the CS-(small effect size), and increased affect ratings to both the CS-(medium effect size) and the CS+ (large effect size) compared to healthy participants. In addition to the effects observed for both patients with anxiety/OCD and PTSD, PTSD patients show larger FPS responses to the CS+ and ΔCS.

(3) During extinction recall, that examines the persistence of extinction learning, the results parallel those of the extinction phase, showing higher ratings of affect and expectancy for the CStogether with increased affect ratings to the CS+ in patients with anxiety-and stress-related disorders compared to healthy participants (medium effect sizes).

(4) In general, the observed heterogeneity was often considerable; however, the number of studies was frequently insufficient for more in-depth moderator analyses. The reinforcement rate and trait anxiety symptoms moderated responding to the ΔCS during the acquisition phase.

Specifically, we found that both the presence of greater differences in anxiety symptoms between groups, as well as a higher reinforcement rate was associated with a smaller differentiation of CS+ and CS-(measured with SCR and FPS, respectively). The full model including the outliers revealed additional moderating influences related to US type, CS type, and depressive symptoms during both acquisition and extinction. Furthermore, it is essential to highlight that the analyses indicated a risk of publication bias, which could lead to distortions and overestimations of the findingsparticularly concerning affect and expectancy ratings during acquisition, as well as SCR and US expectancy during extinction.

In the following sections, we will discuss central findings of our meta-analysis, including the heightened reactivity of anxiety patients to the safety cue CS-during acquisition and extinction, along with their sustained exaggerated response to the CS+ during acquisition, extinction and extinction recall in affective rating results. The heightened responses to a safe stimulus (CS-) that has not been directly associated with an aversive outcome, observed at both physiological and self-report levels during acquisition and extinction, not only replicates but also strengthens findings from prior studies (Craske et al., 2012;Lissek et al., 2009) and the meta-analysis by Duits et al. (2015). Effects sizes of the increased responding to the CS-during acquisition were small to medium (FPS and US expectancy ratings: g = 0.29; affect rating: g = 0.36) and comparable to those reported by Duits et al. (d = 0.30). Importantly, this effect persists during extinction in which patients with stress-related and anxiety disorders continue to show increased responding towards the CS-in affect and expectancy ratings in our study (US expectancy ratings: g = 0.19; affect rating: g = 0.37), an effect similarly seen in Duits et al for subjective ratings (d = 0.26). Our analyses extend these findings and demonstrate that, even in extinction recall, patients with anxiety-related and stress-related disorders subjectively evaluate the CS-as more threatening (US expectancy ratings: g = 0.37; affect rating: g = 0.30). Several underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon have been discussed including impaired safety learning, deficient fear inhibition to stimuli signaling safety, or fear overgeneralization (Beckers et al., 2023;Duits et al., 2015;Jovanovic et al., 2012;Lissek et al., 2005). Overall, the findings of this meta-analysis indicate that heightened responses to the safe cue are present across various stress-related and anxiety disorders, including OCD, and remain stable throughout different phases of fear conditioning experiments, persisting even during extinction. For patients with stress-related and anxiety-related disorders, this results in a diminished ability to recognize safety cues, which can lead to increased uncertainty, stress, arousal, and anxiety, which could contribute to heightened levels of distress (Staples- Bradley et al., 2018) or perception of generalized unsafety (Brosschot et al., 2018). In a broader context, difficulties in discriminating between threat and safety signals are in line with predictive processing frameworks, which posit a common "better-safe-than-sorry" processing strategy as a general vulnerability factor for anxiety or negative affect more broadly (Brosschot et al., 2018;de Jong & Vroling, 2013;Van den Bergh et al., 2021). More specifically, this refers to an information processing heuristic characterized by reduced sensory-perceptual detail, allowing threat-related priors to dominate experience, thereby enhancing the detection of potential threats at the expense of precision (Van den Bergh et al., 2021). In the context of fear conditioning, this phenomenon would manifest as heightened threat responses to stimuli that are, in fact, safe, as indicated by this meta-analysis.

While such a processing mode may be beneficial in threatening environments, it can lead to difficulties in identifying safe stimuli and inhibiting the fear response. Furthermore, whenever a threat is detected, it triggers an immediate, reflexive, associative reaction, followed by a more effortful and deliberate cognitive evaluation process (Buhle et al., 2014;Ouimet et al., 2009;Wen et al., 2024). In conjunction with reduced precision and consequently poorer stimulus discrimination in anxiety-which may increase sensitivity to detecting threats-it appears that the subsequent, more deliberate top-down control over conditioned responses and the inhibition of cued fear, mediated by the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), are also compromised in individuals with anxiety (Sangha et al., 2020). Difficulties in detecting safety stimuli, which contribute to heightened fear responses, combined with impaired ability to inhibit these responses in anxiety-related and stressrelated disorders, may exacerbate symptoms and sustain anxiety in stress-and anxiety-related disorders.

In addition to the aforementioned anomalies in responses to the safety stimulus during acquisition, extinction, and extinction recall, there is also an enhanced aversive evaluation of the CS+ during acquisition, extinction and extinction recall in self-reported affect. These findings align well with and extend the previous findings by Duits and colleagues that report an increased responding to the CS+ for the extinction phase only. Note that effects sizes are larger in our study and of medium -large magnitude (Duits et al,extinction: d = 0.35, our study affect ratings during acquisition: g = 0.52, extinction: g = 0.93, extinction recall: g = 0.46) (Duits et al., 2015). Overall, this supports that individuals with anxiety and stress-related disorders show heightened affective responses to a threatening stimulus (CS+) throughout the various phases of fear conditioning.

Beginning with the acquisition phase, when the fear association is being formed, individuals with anxiety and stress-related disorders report higher affective ratings for the CS+. This finding remains stable even during extinction and extinction recall, despite the CS+ no longer being paired with a threat. This heightened response during extinction has been related to slower extinction processes in anxiety-and stress-related disorder that may contribute to the maintenance and exacerbation of anxiety disorders (Maren & Holmes, 2016;Milad & Quirk, 2012). The inhibitory retrieval model (Craske et al., 2014) postulates that during extinction, the original fear memory remains intact while a new inhibitory memory trace is formed (Bouton, 2004(Bouton, , 2014;;Bouton et al., 2021), and that this inhibitory process is disrupted in anxiety which leads to a dominance of the original fear memory trace. Extinction seems to rely on activity in a neural network centered on the amygdala, the vmPFC, and the hippocampus with a central role of plasticity in the infralimbic cortex as a region within the vmPFC which is important for inhibiting subcortical structures and emotional responses such as fear (Sangha et al., 2020). The inhibitory retrieval model has led to relevant clinical implications for exposure therapy, as reviewed by Craske and colleagues, such as optimizing therapy outcomes by increasing prediction error through expectancy violation and enhancing consolidation (Craske et al., 2022). proceeds (An et al., 2017). This emphasizes the importance of the duration and repetition of exposures in the treatment of anxiety disorders to enhance and sustain the efficacy of exposure therapy. Moreover, targeting multiple learning mechanisms related to extinction learning along with learning across diverse contexts and situations may lead to more stable learning outcomes (Gershman et al., 2010). In addition, several further manipulations have been explored to enhance extinction training, such as pharmacological interventions to disrupt reconsolidation (Kindt et al., 2009), or enhance extinction (Stafford et al., 2012). We focus on extinction learning and the translational insights that can be derived from laboratory studies in this research field for exposurebased interventions. Although this is a significant field of research, it is important to acknowledge that extinction, while presenting an interesting and plausible model for exposure-based therapies, has its limitations (Scheveneels et al., 2016). For example, the types of stimuli and outcome measures differ considerably from those used in clinical exposure procedures, as do the timing factors (e.g., single sessions versus extended learning experiences over several weeks; Kredlow et al., 2022). Moreover, several mechanisms that contribute to the success of exposure therapies are often overlooked in extinction models, including instrumental learning, actively approaching aversive situations, avoidance, habituation, and cognitive factors such as expectation violation (see Benito et al., 2024 andKnowles &Tolin, 2022 for detailed reviews). Future research directions that aim to enhance insights for exposure-based therapies may benefit from utilizing more ecologically valid and complex stimuli, such as the use of virtual reality (Kredlow et al., 2022;Scheveneels et al., 2016). Additionally, it is essential to acknowledge and integrate other relevant mechanisms and their interactions. For instance, sustained fear responses during extinction promote avoidance behavior (Cain, 2019;de Haart et al., 2021;Hunt et al., 2022) which is known to contribute to the maintenance of anxiety and to hinder extinction (Kausche et al., 2022;Pittig et al., 2018). This reinforces and strengthens anxiety-related patterns, potentially expediting the chronicity and increased severity of anxiety disorders. Shedding light on the interplay between fear learning, extinction, and other relevant psychopathological mechanisms such as avoidance is crucial to comprehend the complex processes involved in the development and maintenance of anxiety disorders, to inspire the search for effective interventions.

It is noteworthy that we observed increased responding to both CS+ and CS-across all phases of fear conditioning, resulting in a similar level of discrimination between CS+ and CS-in healthy controls and patients with stress-and anxiety-related disorders. This suggests an overall heightened reactivity to safe and threat cues rather than improved differentiation between safe and threatening cues. This effect may be attributed to generalization (Cooper et al., 2022), general hyperarousal (Grillon, 2008) or increased sensitivity to threat (Naragon-Gainey, 2010), functioning as a cognitive bias in stress-related and anxiety disorders, resulting in exaggerated responses to both threatening and safe stimuli (Chaaya et al., 2018). This heightened reactivity limits the ability to differentiate between CS+ and CS-, reducing the distinction between safe and threatening cues.

Deficits in hippocampus-mediated pattern separation, a process through which memories are encoded as distinct representations, have been proposed as a potential underlying marker for difficulties in differentiation and increased generalization in fear conditioning (Lopresto et al., 2016). Additionally, the emotional context during conditioning may further influence responses to both CS+ and CS-, explaining the exaggerated reactions (Andreatta et al., 2020) and generalization.

In summary, the lack of increased differentiation between CS+ and CS-in anxiety conditioning studies can reflect a broader pattern of heightened reactivity and difficulty in distinguishing between safe and threatening stimuli or context generalization effects. Furthermore, it highlights the possibility that relying solely on difference measures in conditioning studies may obscure a general alteration in response tendencies.

While the subgroup analyses generally support the reported pattern of results for both patients with PTSD and those with anxiety disorders and OCD, certain differential effects must be noted. Specifically, the observed effects were significantly stronger in individuals with anxiety disorders and OCD during the acquisition phase. Follow-up subgroup analyses indicate that the heightened affective ratings in response to the CS+ during acquisition are specific to anxiety disorders and OCD. Furthermore, only patients with anxiety disorders and OCD exhibited heightened SCR to the ΔCS, while patients with PTSD did not show these effects. Additionally, effect sizes for stronger CS-responding during acquisition in the PTSD group were small (US expectancy g = 0.12; affect rating g = 0.17), whereas effect sizes were significantly higher and of medium size for anxiety disorders and OCD (US expectancy g = 0.58; affect rating g = 0.47). In contrast, during the extinction phase, larger effects were observed in PTSD patients, with alterations in fear-potentiated startle-specifically, a stronger startle response to the CS+ and ΔCS manifesting only in patients with PTSD, revealing medium to strong effect sizes. These effects were not apparent in patients with anxiety disorders or OCD. Overall, the pattern of results suggests that there are more alterations during the acquisition phase in anxiety patients and OCD, while stronger effects appear during extinction in PTSD patients. However, it remains unclear whether this finding is replicable. Notably, this differential effect was not reported in the analyses conducted by Duits et al., underscoring the need for future studies to further investigate this effect, its robustness, and its implications for treatment. Phenomenologically, it may align with the notion that the symptomatology in PTSD typically begins after an extremely intense learning event and life stressor, such as a trauma, which would be significant for everyone. In contrast, anxiety patients often seem to lack clear initial learning experiences, which may be related to heightened sensitivity and altered processes in the acquisition of fear. These findings may contribute to the existing literature that emphasizes both shared and distinct psychopathological processes in fear conditioning between PTSD and anxiety disorders (Acheson et al., 2015), as well as differences in brain structure (Radua et al., 2010), and etiological factors (Chantarujikapong et al., 2001). Overall, there are only a few studies that directly compare different disorders with each other, and more studies in this area would be desirable. Similarly, a network meta-analysis that enables direct and indirect disorder comparisons could enhance future insights into group comparisons. Given the current data situation, this would only be possible through aggregation across different outcomes.

Even after considering subgroups, there remains a high degree of heterogeneity in the findings. Subgroup analyses in the full dataset including outliers support the notion that some of this heterogeneity is likely attributable to methodological factors, such as US type, CS type, and reinforcement rate-all of which have previously been linked to differences in fear conditioning (e.g., Ahs et al., 2018;Lonsdorf et al., 2017;Ney et al., 2022). In addition, participant diversity, symptom variability, and reliance on diagnostic categories that exhibit high comorbidity and heterogeneity likely also contribute to the overall heterogeneity. Dimensional analyses regarding differences in trait anxiety and depressive symptoms between clinical groups and healthy participants in primary studies in this meta-analysis suggest that higher symptom severity in trait anxiety was associated with larger SCR responses to the ΔCS during acquisition. Note, that the effects of differences in depressive symptoms were observed in the full model, including outliers, linking depressive symptoms to changes in fear learning processes (Luo et al., 2024;Otto et al., 2014). More precisely, without excluding outliers, we found that larger differences in depressive symptoms between the clinical groups and healthy participant groups were linked to decreased ΔCS in affect ratings, which was driven by increased affect ratings to the CS-and descriptively decreased affect ratings to the CS+. In the acquisition phase, the full models including outliers indicated that increased depressive symptoms were associated with increased SCR to CS+. Of note, only a subset of studies reported differences in depressive symptoms, thus this pattern of results requires further investigation. Collectively, the results indicate that differences in depressive symptoms between groups might modulate SCR during acquisition and affect ratings during extinction, highlighting the need to move beyond comparing different disorder categories and consider the complex heterogeneous nature of mental disorders and their co-occurrence using dimensional analyses. However, due to heterogeneity in reported clinical measures in primary studies, our data did not sufficiently allow for more detailed analyses of specific transdiagnostic symptom dimension associations. Therefore, we cannot conclusively determine whether the observed patterns of results are specifically related to certain symptom profiles or more broadly linked to anxiety. Furthermore, our results have been identified in the context of heterogeneous often multisymptomatic patients having comorbid diagnoses, thus it appears promising to reclassify patients based on their dysfunctions in fear conditioning and extinction (Fyer et al., 2020). The exploration of data-driven subtypes has the potential to elucidate associations with symptomatology at a more granular level and simplify the complexity of analyses by providing clearly defined subtypes to delve deeper into the neurobiological foundations of these dysfunctions. Furthermore, it offers the opportunity to personalize treatment based on observed aberrancies in fear learning processes, e.g., focusing on improving discriminating between threat and safety signals or enhancing extinction learning. This approach may ultimately inform the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies.

Overall, the analysis reveals more effects in the realm of subjective ratings, particularly in affective evaluations, while physiological effects were only seen for FPS responses to the CSduring acquisition, as well as exaggerated FPS responding to CS+ and ΔCS in PTSD. This underscores the distinction between different anxiety systems and the discrepancy between subjective ratings and physiological responses. In the context of our data we observed most robust differences on a self-report level, and only robust alterations in fear potentiated startle during CSresponding during acquisition. The two-system framework by LeDoux and Pine (2016) can be used to explain these differences. Based on this theory, the used outcome measurements may reflect different processes of fear learning. The framework distinguishes between two processes involving distinct neural regions: the conscious experience of "fear," mainly mediated by cortical areas, and the automatic behavioral and physiological responses to threats, predominantly controlled by subcortical regions such as the amygdala. This differentiation is supported by a meta-analysis showing distinct neural mechanisms underlying explicit (involving the pulvinar and parahippocampal gyrus) and implicit fear processing (involving a cerebellum-amygdala-cortical pathway) (Tao et al., 2021). Furthermore, a recent study examining the correspondence of physiological activity and arousal and valence rating using representational similarity analysis (RSA) supports that similar affective experiences are related to distinct physiological responses, emphasizing divergence of physiological and self-report data and the importance of considering intra-individual variability (Koppold et al., 2024). Notably, no robust group differences were observed for SCR, which are among of the most commonly used outcome measures in fear conditioning studies. This finding contributes to existing research highlighting the high methodological heterogeneity in SCR studies (Sjouwerman et al., 2022), which may limit both reliability and validity.

In summary, this meta-analysis strengthens and expands the central findings of Duits by revealing heightened responses especially to safety cues during initial learning, as well as its persistence after extinction in stress-and anxiety-related disorders. Conceptually, it is evident that alterations in fear and safety learning are frequently regarded as risk or vulnerability markers in research studies and psychopathological models, contributing to the onset and persistence of stressand anxiety-related disorders. These are seen as enduring traits of an individual that predate the disorder and contribute to its emergence, as well as predicting the course of the disorder and response to treatment. However, most studies conducted thus far are cross-sectional, which limits conclusions about causality and predictability. Thus, differences in acquisition/extinction/extinction recall may either be a consequence of anxiety and stress symptomatology, a risk factor, or both.

Furthermore, several important prerequisites for a marker to be considered a reliable vulnerability indicator or endophenotype have not been tested (Gottesman & Goud, 2003;Miller & Rockstroh, 2013). It is essential to demonstrate that alterations are present before the onset of the disorder and in individuals at increased risk for developing the disorder, such as in unaffected first-degree relatives. To the best of our knowledge, this has not yet been tested in the field of fear conditioning.

Furthermore, a vulnerability marker should possess predictive validity to forecast the course of symptoms. There are few studies examining the predictive validity for the onset of symptoms and treatment trajectories. A longitudinal investigation that supports predictive validity showed that a weaker neural discrimination between the CS+ and CS-in vmPFC during fear acquisition was associated with a greater increase in fear symptoms over the next 2.5 years (Peng et al., 2023).

Further, as reviewed by Scheveneels et al. results suggest that reduced extinction and broader generalization predict higher anxiety levels (Scheveneels et al., 2021). In relation to the predictive validity of alterations in fear conditioning for treatment outcome, only a very limited number of studies did examine this with some studies do find an association with extinction and therapy outcome whereas others do not (Scheveneels et al., 2021). Several studies have established a connection between changes in fear conditioning and therapeutic success, especially within the framework of exposure therapy. In the case of spider phobia, an association was shown between pre-treatment differences in fear ratings for CS+ and CS-and symptom reductions. Further, differences in extinction learning in OCD were linked to CBT outcome (Geller et al., 2019). A twin study on monozygotic twins discordant for combat exposure and PTSD suggests that deficient retention of extinction in conditioned fear occurs only in those with PTSD not their co-twins, supporting the conclusion that this deficit is a result of combat trauma leading to PTSD, rather than a predisposing factor shared within families (Milad et al., 2008). This highlights environmental factors and learning experiences as sources of variation in fear learning, which is further supported by a recent meta-analysis suggesting that adverse childhood experiences lead to diminished CS+/CS-discrimination during acquisition and generalization, driven by decreased responses to CS+ (Ruge et al., 2024). In summary, the empirical basis for evaluating changes in fear conditioning as vulnerability markers for anxiety, PTSD, and OCD is insufficient and does not support this far-reaching perspective. Future studies incorporating high-risk studies and longitudinal designs, along with a more cautious approach to assumptions of causality, are both necessary and important.

div.head: Limitations and recommendation for future studies
div.p: There are some limitations to our meta-analysis. First, the study selection may have introduced a bias, as only published studies were included and several studies had to be excluded due to insufficient details for calculating effect sizes. Second, we included only studies that used a patient sample based on a clinical interview. However, there was no information of clinical expertise, why there is the possibility of insufficient clinical expertise in the diagnosis depending on the clinical training as a potential limitation of the validity of disorder diagnosis. Third, there are some indications of publication bias, which may have led to an overestimation of effect sizes and biases in the reporting of results, and which may have even underestimated the effects since only published studies were considered. Although, results of our Egger's test and p-curve analyses indicate different fields for publication bias, which limits interpretation of publication bias. Fourth, the heterogeneity was substantial, and the number of outliers was relatively high. While their exclusion in our main models increased robustness, it may have introduced bias due to the removal of several studies. Therefore, we also reported the model without outlier removal in the supplementary materials and highlighted discrepancies in the main paper. Additionally, many influences in the moderator analyses could not be computed due to the limited number of studies remaining for specific moderators, especially after outlier exclusion. Once again, the effects of outlier exclusion are detailed in the supplement and referenced in the paper. In this context, we would like to refer once again to the information in our tables 2 and 3, in which the heterogeneity between the studies and the difficulty of reconciling them becomes apparent. Our meta-analysis highlights the substantial heterogeneity across studies, encompassing variations in study design, stimulus type (CS and US), the number of stimulus presentations. In addition, reading through the primary studies, it becomes apparent that even if the same outcome measurements were used, their application and processing differed between studies. These differences pose a significant challenge to synthesizing results and deriving clear conclusions, particularly when aiming to explore nuanced aspects such as the characteristics of different anxiety disorders. This between-study heterogeneity underscores the pressing need for greater standardization in fear conditioning research. Future studies should strive to align methodologies, including standardized protocols for stimulus presentation, measurement, and analysis, to facilitate more meaningful comparisons and advance our understanding of the mechanisms underlying anxiety disorders. Without such harmonization, the interpretability and applicability of meta-analytic findings remain limited, potentially hindering progress in the field. Also, only some studies provided information about medication. So we could not include this as a possible moderator in our analyses, why we cannot rule out the possibility of medication influencing our results. Moreover, there are additional variables (e.g., specific symptom dimensions of anxiety, symptom severity, and assessment of functioning) that could explain variance across studies but were not systematically assessed in a similar manner across studies and therefore could not be examined. This highlights the need to define and adhere to standards in studying fear conditioning (Bach et al., 2023;Lonsdorf et al., 2017). Moreover, investigating fear learning processes on a trial-by-trial basis would give the possibility to investigate a more dynamic aspect of fear learning. Furthermore, the study focuses on laboratory studies of fear conditioning using aversive stimulations like shocks or sounds, limiting the ecological validity of studies while maximizing internal validity. Future studies could increase the ecological validity by using scenarios or stimuli that more closely resemble the symptoms or daily life. A further step could be the use of experience sampling method (ESM) or ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to offer valuable insights into the temporal dynamics of fear responses and their fluctuations over time in naturalistic environments (Verhagen et al., 2016), and help to capture individual variability in fear responses and conditioning processes (Vries et al., 2001). In addition, the strength of this metaanalysis lies in a comprehensive integration and summary of findings across studies, which, however, limits the resolution and inferences regarding the underlying processes and mechanisms that could not be integrated within this study. Nonetheless, it can guide the direction of future research by identifying which processes are consistently altered and which mechanisms require further elucidation. Finally, drawing from the insights garnered during the meta-analysis process,
we have outlined the primary challenges encountered and formulated recommendations for future research (table 7).

div.head: Challenge Recommendation
div.p: Studies lack reporting relevant descriptive statistics or parameter estimates of the analyses.

-Include descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviations) for all outcome measurements. -Authors are encouraged to share or publish their data, in line with the open science movement (Branney et al., 2023;Renkewitz & Heene, 2019).
Hyperfocus on categorical diagnoses with limited use of questionnaires that allow for transdiagnostic analyses.
-Use measurements that facilitate dimensional analyses (e.g. Cross-D, Lebeau et al., 2012;4DSQ, Terluin et al., 2006).
High degree of heterogeneity in the questionnaires used or in the assessed moderator variables (e.g., symptom severity, assessment of functioning).

-Utilization of standard questionnaires to promote integration across studies, (e.g. PHQ-9 (Kroenke et al., 2001), OCI-R (Foa et al., 2002;Gonner et al., 2007)) -Use and report standardization techniques like ztransformation to convert values into a common scale, facilitating the comparison and integration of results
Heterogeneity in terminology and research design when studying fear conditioning restricts comparability across studies.

- -To capture the complexity of fear conditioning, researchers should investigate a range of outcome measures to encompass the multiple facets of fear conditioning Different outcome measurements require specific timings (Lonsdorf et al., 2017), which can lead to interference or alterations when recorded simultaneously -Employ optimized designs for your dependent variables -If needed limit the number of outcomes -report results for all outcome measurements Outcome measures differ in reliability and precision limiting the validity of results -Report reliability or precision estimated for all outcome measures (i.e, questionnaires, ratings, physiological and neural outcomes)

Our meta-analysis integrated fear conditioning studies focusing on fear and safety learning in individuals with stress-relates and anxiety disorders and OCD. The results demonstrated heightened reactivity to safety cues during acquisition, extinction and extinction recall, supported by both verbal self-report and during acquisition also startle results. Additionally, individuals with stressand anxiety-related disorders exhibited sustained exaggerated responses to threatening cues (CS+)
during acquisition that sustain during extinction and extinction recall, as indicated by affect ratings.

Effect sizes were generally small to medium. While alterations during acquisition were more pronounced (i.e. CS-responding) or even limited (CS+ responding) to anxiety and OCD, extinction effects were pronounced in PTSD. Given the considerable heterogeneity and signs of publication bias, as well as the predominance of results in self-report measures, caution is advised in drawing definitive conclusions. Further, the rather moderate support for alterations in fear and safety learning in PTSD, OCD and anxiety stands in contrast to the importance of these changes within many models of the onset and treatment of stress-related and anxiety disorders and underscores the necessity to expand our research to explore additional mechanisms and processes to understand and treat stress-and anxiety-related disorders. Overall, across studies, a small but consistent increase in responding to safety cues (CS-) is observed in stress-and anxiety-related disorders during acquisition, extinction and extinction recall, alongside a heightened response to threat cues (CS+) across these phases, suggesting resistance to extinction. These patterns underscore how stress-and anxiety-related disorders involve alterations in both threat and safety detection and fear regulation.
